description: Labeled evaluation cases for the AI-assisted session review feature (docs/BUILD_PLAN.md, 'Planned AI feature'). Each case is a completed Session record paired with the signals a correct structured review draft must surface. See docs/eval/README.md for how to score against these.

session.explanation_checkpoint: I understand the model, storage, CLI, and completion gate.

strengths: acceptance criteria (all tests pass) is directly supported by the evidence (14 passed, 0 failed)
constraint (stdlib only) is not contradicted by anything in evidence or explanation
risks: explanation checkpoint names the components touched but does not describe any specific tradeoff or design decision, so depth of understanding is only partially demonstrated
next_action ('Write the first test') reads as though testing has not started yet, which is inconsistent with evidence showing 14 tests already passing
follow_ups: ask the learner to explain one specific tradeoff (e.g. why stdlib-only, what it ruled out)
clarify or correct next_action so it reflects the actual next step post-completion
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Evidence directly supports acceptance criteria, but the next_action/evidence inconsistency and shallow explanation prevent high confidence.

cases.notes: Real record from sessions/demo.json. Baseline case: evidence supports the criteria, but two real inconsistencies (shallow explanation, stale next_action) should not be missed just because the surface result looks clean.

session.acceptance_criteria: Able to POST and GET values
session.explanation_checkpoint: Testing POST and GET is working as expected.

strengths: evidence topic (POST and GET) matches acceptance criteria topic
risks: evidence is an unverified claim, not proof: no test output, request/response example, or tool used to confirm 'is working'
explanation checkpoint restates the evidence/goal rather than demonstrating understanding of how or why it works
constraints ('Full stack') is far broader than what evidence covers (only POST/GET), and nothing (DB, UI, auth) is addressed
next_action ('Plan the stack') suggests the stack wasn't chosen yet, contradicting a full-stack CRUD app being marked completed
follow_ups: request concrete evidence: command run, output, or a request/response transcript
ask what 'full stack' currently covers vs. still needs (data layer, UI, auth)
reconcile next_action with completed status
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Evidence and explanation are both unverifiable claims rather than demonstrated proof, and scope (full stack) is not covered by what was described.

cases.notes: Real record from sessions/practice.json. Tests whether the review catches 'evidence' that is just an assertion, and a constraints/evidence scope mismatch.

session.constraints: Use Python standard library only, no third-party packages
session.acceptance_criteria: CLI prints current temperature for a given city
session.evidence: Ran `python -m weather_cli --city Honolulu`; used the `requests` library to call the weather API; printed '84F'.
session.explanation_checkpoint: requests made the HTTP call simple, so I used it instead of urllib.
session.next_action: Add error handling for invalid city names

strengths: acceptance criteria (prints current temperature) is directly demonstrated by the evidence output
risks: constraint violation: evidence and explanation both state `requests` (a third-party package) was used, directly contradicting the stdlib-only constraint
follow_ups: flag the constraint violation explicitly and ask whether to rewrite with urllib or update the constraint
do not mark this a clean pass despite acceptance criteria being met, since a constraint was broken
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: The violation is explicit and unambiguous in the learner's own explanation, not inferred.

cases.notes: Tests whether the review prioritizes an explicit constraint violation over surface-level acceptance-criteria success. This is the most important failure mode to catch reliably.

session.goal: Add a logout button to the settings page
session.acceptance_criteria: Clicking logout clears the session and redirects to /login
session.evidence: Manual test: clicked logout, session cookie cleared, redirected to /login as expected.
session.explanation_checkpoint: The button calls the existing logout() handler already used elsewhere, then does a client-side redirect.

strengths: evidence directly demonstrates the acceptance criteria via a concrete manual test
explanation shows understanding of reuse (existing logout() handler) rather than a black-box claim
risks: evidence is manual only, no automated test — acceptable for a one-off UI change but worth naming as a gap
next_action is empty, which is valid per the schema but means there is no recorded follow-up even though this is a small, easily regression-tested change
follow_ups: suggest an automated test (e.g. a UI or integration test for the logout flow) as a low-cost next_action
do not treat the empty next_action as an error — the schema allows it — but note the missed opportunity
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Evidence is credible and specific, but manual-only testing plus no recorded next step slightly limits confidence.

cases.notes: Tests handling of a schema-valid but empty next_action field — the review should not fabricate a violation, but should still note the gap.

session.acceptance_criteria: POST /reset-password sends a reset link and updates the password on confirmation
session.evidence: curl POST /reset-password returns 200 and an email is received with a working reset link; confirmed password updates after clicking the link.
session.explanation_checkpoint: The endpoint generates a token, emails a link containing it, and the confirm endpoint checks the token before allowing the update.

strengths: acceptance criteria is demonstrated end-to-end with a concrete manual trace (request, email, confirmation)
risks: no mention of token expiry, single-use enforcement, or rate limiting on the reset endpoint — all standard requirements for password-reset flows and a plausible security gap the evidence/explanation is silent on
no automated test evidence, only a manual curl trace, for a security-sensitive endpoint
follow_ups: ask explicitly whether the reset token expires and is single-use before deploying to staging
recommend automated tests for the security-relevant edge cases (expired token, reused token, wrong token) before next_action proceeds
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Functional path is shown, but the review cannot confirm safety-critical properties (expiry, single-use) that are neither confirmed nor denied by the record.

cases.notes: Tests whether the review flags an absent security property rather than only checking what's explicitly stated. This is a 'silence is a risk' case, harder than an explicit contradiction.

session.goal: Refactor the pricing calculator to support discount codes
session.constraints: No changes to the public calculate_price() signature
session.acceptance_criteria: calculate_price() applies a discount code when valid and ignores invalid ones
session.explanation_checkpoint: I refactored the pricing calculator to support discount codes.

strengths: test evidence (9 passed) is concrete and scoped to the relevant test file
risks: explanation checkpoint is a restatement of the goal, not an explanation — it gives no indication the learner understands how discount validation works or how the signature constraint was preserved
no evidence that the public signature constraint was actually respected (no diff, no mention of it)
follow_ups: ask the learner to explain specifically how invalid codes are detected and how the signature was kept unchanged
this should not be treated as passing the explanation-checkpoint intent even though the field is non-empty
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Test evidence is solid, but the explanation checkpoint fails its purpose (demonstrating understanding), which the review must catch even though the field is technically filled in.

cases.notes: Tests whether the review distinguishes 'field is non-empty' (passes the Session.complete() gate) from 'field actually satisfies its purpose' — the completion gate is a floor, not a quality check, and the review must apply real judgment on top of it.

session.goal: Fix the off-by-one error in the pagination component
session.evidence: python -m pytest tests/test_pagination.py: 22 passed. Also rewrote the pagination component to use a new library and updated 6 other components that depended on it.
session.explanation_checkpoint: Fixed the off-by-one bug and while I was in there, modernized the whole pagination system since it looked outdated.
session.next_action: Update documentation for the new pagination API

strengths: test evidence for the specific off-by-one fix appears present (22 tests passed)
risks: constraint says 'minimal, targeted fix' but evidence and explanation both describe a full rewrite touching 6 other components — a direct constraint violation via scope creep
wider blast radius (6 dependent components) increases regression risk without evidence those components were individually verified
follow_ups: flag the scope-creep as a constraint violation regardless of whether tests pass
ask for evidence that each of the 6 dependent components was tested, not just the pagination component itself
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: The constraint violation is explicit and self-reported in the explanation checkpoint.

cases.notes: A second constraint-violation flavor distinct from case-03: this one is about scope discipline rather than a technology/library restriction. Tests that the review doesn't reward extra unrequested work as a strength.

session.goal: Add input validation to the signup form
session.constraints: Client-side only for now, server-side validation is a separate ticket
session.acceptance_criteria: Empty email, invalid email format, and short passwords are all rejected with an inline error
session.evidence: Manually tested empty email and invalid email format, both show inline errors correctly.
session.explanation_checkpoint: Added regex-based email validation and a required-field check; ran out of time to test the password length case but the code path looks the same as the email checks.

strengths: two of the three acceptance-criteria conditions (empty email, invalid format) are directly demonstrated
explanation checkpoint is honest and specific about what was and wasn't verified
risks: acceptance criteria requires three conditions; only two are evidenced. The third (short passwords) is explicitly unverified, so the session should not be treated as fully meeting its acceptance criteria
'looks the same as the email checks' is an assumption, not evidence
follow_ups: do not report acceptance criteria as fully met; state clearly that 1 of 3 conditions is unverified
next_action already correctly targets the gap — reinforce that this must happen before considering the feature done, not just as a nice-to-have
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Honest, specific partial evidence lets the review pinpoint the exact gap with confidence, even though the feature overall is incomplete relative to its stated criteria.

cases.notes: Tests whether the review correctly scores partial acceptance-criteria coverage rather than treating 'evidence exists' as 'criteria met'. Also rewards an honest gap disclosure rather than penalizing it as harshly as a hidden one.

session.goal: Migrate the database schema for the orders table
session.acceptance_criteria: Migration applies cleanly and all existing order records remain queryable afterward
session.evidence: Ran migration up: 3 tests failed (order_total precision), 12 passed. Ran migration down successfully.
session.explanation_checkpoint: The migration changes the order_total column type and is reversible, confirmed by running it down successfully.
session.next_action: Fix the precision issue in order_total

strengths: the down-migration (reversibility constraint) is demonstrated and passes
explanation and next_action are consistent with the evidence about the precision issue
risks: acceptance criteria requires the migration to 'apply cleanly', but evidence shows 3 failing tests on the up-migration — the record is marked completed despite the primary acceptance criterion not being met
this is the clearest case where evidence text is present (satisfying the completion gate) but does not actually support the acceptance criteria
follow_ups: explicitly state that this session should not be considered to have met its acceptance criteria, despite passing Session.complete()'s non-empty-field check
the next_action correctly targets the real gap, so validate rather than duplicate it
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: The contradiction (3 failing tests vs. 'applies cleanly' criteria) is stated plainly in the evidence field itself.

cases.notes: The sharpest illustration of why Session.complete()'s non-empty-string gate is not a correctness gate: this record is schema-valid and 'completed' while its own evidence field documents test failures against the stated acceptance criteria.

session.acceptance_criteria: Search results look better and load faster
session.evidence: Changed results to a card layout and added lazy image loading; page feels snappier when scrolling.
session.explanation_checkpoint: Card layout is more modern and lazy loading avoids loading all images upfront.
session.next_action: Get design feedback on the new layout

strengths: the two named changes (card layout, lazy loading) plausibly map to the two vague criteria (looks better, loads faster)
risks: acceptance criteria itself is unmeasurable as written ('looks better', 'faster' with no baseline or metric), which is a criteria-quality problem the review should name, not just a session-evidence problem
'feels snappier' is a subjective impression, not a measurement (no load-time numbers, no before/after)
follow_ups: recommend the acceptance criteria be rewritten with a measurable bar (e.g. a specific load-time target or a defined design spec) for future sessions on this goal
suggest capturing an actual load-time measurement before/after as evidence, not just a subjective impression
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Vague acceptance criteria makes it impossible to confidently judge whether the criteria was met at all, independent of evidence quality.

cases.notes: Tests whether the review can diagnose a problem with the input itself (unmeasurable acceptance criteria) rather than only ever critiquing the evidence against a criteria bar it assumes is well-formed.

session.goal: Add rate limiting to the public API
session.constraints: Use the existing Redis instance for counters
session.acceptance_criteria: Requests beyond 100/min per API key return 429
session.evidence: Load-tested with 150 requests/min from one key; first 100 succeeded, remaining 50 returned 429 as expected.
session.explanation_checkpoint: Rate limiting uses a sliding window counter in Redis keyed by API key.
session.next_action: Write a load test to confirm the 429 behavior at the 100/min threshold

strengths: evidence directly and quantitatively demonstrates the acceptance criteria (429 after 100/min)
explanation shows a specific implementation detail (sliding window, Redis-keyed) rather than a generic claim
risks: next_action asks to write a load test to confirm 429 behavior, but the evidence shows that load test was already performed and passed — the next_action is stale/redundant
follow_ups: flag that next_action appears to duplicate work already completed per the evidence field, and should be corrected or replaced with a genuinely new next step
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Both the acceptance-criteria match and the next_action redundancy are unambiguous from the record's own text.

cases.notes: Otherwise a strong record — tests whether the review still catches a smaller-stakes inconsistency (stale next_action) even when the core evidence/criteria match is clean, rather than stopping analysis once the main criterion looks satisfied.

session.goal: Add unit tests for the tax calculation module
session.constraints: Cover at least the edge cases listed in the ticket (zero income, negative income, multiple brackets)
session.acceptance_criteria: All three named edge cases have a passing test
session.explanation_checkpoint: Added tests for the tax module.

strengths: a test run with a pass count is at least real, executable evidence, unlike a purely verbal claim
risks: evidence gives a pass count (7) but no way to confirm the three specifically named edge cases (zero income, negative income, multiple brackets) are actually among them
explanation checkpoint is generic and does not name which edge cases were covered, so it cannot corroborate the evidence either
follow_ups: ask for the specific test names or a coverage report to confirm the three named edge cases are covered, since a pass count alone does not prove it
next_action (review coverage report) is a reasonable way to close this gap — validate it rather than treating this session as already fully verified
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: The acceptance criteria names specific required cases, and neither evidence nor explanation confirms those specific cases were tested, only that some tests exist and pass.

cases.notes: A distinct flavor of vague evidence from case-02/case-06: here the evidence is real (an actual test run) but too coarse-grained to verify the specific, named acceptance criteria.

session.goal: Refactor the entire order-processing pipeline to use async I/O
session.constraints: No change to the public OrderProcessor API; must remain backward compatible
session.acceptance_criteria: All existing integration tests pass and average processing latency drops by at least 30%
session.explanation_checkpoint: Converted the pipeline to use asyncio for I/O-bound steps.

strengths: 'tests pass' at least claims the compatibility half of the acceptance criteria was checked
risks: for a change of this size (entire pipeline refactor), 'tests pass' is far too thin — no test count, no indication which suite, no confirmation the public API was actually left unchanged

acceptance criteria has two parts (tests pass AND latency drops 30%); only the first is even claimed, and the second is explicitly deferred to next_action — this session should not be treated as having met its acceptance criteria yet
follow_ups: state plainly that only half of a two-part acceptance criteria has any evidence at all, and the 30% latency target is entirely unverified
given the size of the change (entire pipeline), ask for a specific test count and confirmation of API backward-compatibility, not just 'tests pass'
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: The evidence-to-change-size ratio is very poor, and one of two explicit acceptance-criteria components is unaddressed.

cases.notes: Tests whether the review calibrates evidence sufficiency to the size/risk of the change, not just to whether the evidence field is non-empty and vaguely positive.

session.goal: Add a retry mechanism for flaky external API calls
session.constraints: Exponential backoff, max 3 retries, must not retry on 4xx responses
session.acceptance_criteria: 5xx and network errors are retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff; 4xx errors are not retried
session.explanation_checkpoint: I wrote a decorator that catches ConnectionError and 5xx responses, retries with backoff of 1s/2s/4s up to 3 times, and re-raises immediately on any 4xx since those are treated as non-retryable client errors per the ticket.
session.next_action: Apply the decorator to the two other integrations that need it

strengths: explanation checkpoint is detailed and precisely matches every clause of the constraints and acceptance criteria (backoff schedule, retry cap, 4xx exclusion)
next_action is a sensible, concrete follow-up
risks: only 4 tests for a feature with several distinct required behaviors (5xx retried, network-error retried, 4xx not retried, backoff timing, retry cap) — plausible but not confirmed that each behavior has its own test versus a few tests covering only some paths
evidence gives no detail on what the 4 tests actually assert
follow_ups: ask for the test names or a brief description of what each of the 4 tests covers, to confirm the 4xx non-retry behavior specifically has a test (it's the easiest behavior to accidentally leave unverified)
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: The explanation is strong enough to raise confidence despite thin evidence, but a low test count relative to the number of distinct required behaviors keeps this from being high confidence.

cases.notes: Tests whether the review can hold two different signals in tension (strong explanation vs. thin test evidence) rather than anchoring on just one field. Also the intended positive-control case for the 'confidence' field: it should land in the middle, not at an extreme.

session.goal: Write a script to rename files in a folder by prefix
session.acceptance_criteria: Running the script renames all .txt files in the target folder with the given prefix
session.evidence: Ran on a test folder with 3 .txt files and 1 .csv file; all 3 .txt files were renamed with the prefix, the .csv file was untouched.
session.explanation_checkpoint: The script filters files by extension before renaming, so non-.txt files are skipped.
session.next_action: Add a --dry-run flag before using this on real folders

strengths: evidence is specific and directly tests the exact scenario in the acceptance criteria, including the negative case (.csv file untouched)
explanation correctly identifies the mechanism (extension filter) responsible for the observed behavior
next_action (dry-run flag) shows good judgment about the risk of an irreversible file-renaming operation, even though nothing in the goal/constraints asked for it
risks: constraints field is empty, so there is nothing to check the evidence against beyond the acceptance criteria itself — this is schema-valid but worth noting as a thin input, not a flaw in the work performed
follow_ups: none required for correctness; optionally suggest recording a constraint for scripts that mutate the filesystem (e.g. 'must support dry-run') going forward
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Evidence, explanation, and even an unrequested safety consideration (dry-run) are all mutually consistent and well-scoped to a small, well-tested change.

cases.notes: The other clean positive case (alongside case-01), but with an empty optional-in-practice field (constraints) to make sure the review doesn't manufacture a risk out of an empty field when the rest of the record is genuinely solid.

session.goal: Add dark mode support to the dashboard
session.constraints: Use CSS variables, no new dependencies
session.acceptance_criteria: Toggling dark mode updates all dashboard components without a page reload
session.evidence: Converted the header and sidebar to use CSS variables; toggle works for those two components.
session.next_action: Convert the remaining chart and table components to use CSS variables

risks: status is 'active', not 'completed' — this record should not be run through the completed-session review flow at all
follow_ups: the feature should reject or defer this input rather than generate a review draft for an in-progress session
expected_signals.confidence_rationale: Not applicable: this case tests input validation/routing (reject non-completed sessions), not review quality.

cases.notes: Precondition/guard-rail case, not a review-quality case: the review-generation code path should only ever run on status == 'completed' sessions (this is also schema-consistent with Session.complete()'s explanation_checkpoint requirement being unmet here). Use this to test the feature's input guard, separate from the SDK-response failure-mode tests (valid/malformed/refused/timed-out) already planned in docs/TASKS.md.
